Perfect willpower, methodical application, and pain endurance. It's an incredible feeling to have power over self, to only do what you really want to do and not be enslaved by passions and paying the debt of regret. 

This has instilled in me an inner peace and fulfillment.  Whereas previously relative comparisons would leave me feeling dismayed, that is now out of my peripheral vision. I'm self-satisfied with my absolute conditions of life. 

Our society is pretty messed up right now with people making money when they seduce you into doing things against your best interest, which then reflexively forces you to justify your actions as good, because how else is one to cope and reconcile the situation? 

Wherever your at in life, I want to lend you a helping hand and offer words of encouragement.  You can be epic while being healthy. People have this mistaken idea that one must be unhealthy in order to be successful. It's one of the corrosive ideas of this early 21st century. 

You don't need to do much. Master the basics and avoid the really bad stuff and you'll be in a good spot.

People consuming the most artificial sweeteners showed 63% faster cognitive decline than those consuming the least, roughly equivalent to 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging.

The middle-intake group also showed a 36% faster decline, equivalent to about 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.

That’s from a Neurology study following 12,772 adults for about eight years. And when researchers looked separately by age, the association showed up in people under 60, but not those 60 and older.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
I get asked a lot about magnesium supplements. Here are my general thoughts.

Start with magnesium-rich foods - leafy greens, nuts, seeds, and legumes. Supplements can help when your diet falls short.

Citrate, glycinate/bisglycinate, and chloride are good options. Citrate and chloride are generally better absorbed than oxide. Malate and taurate are alternatives. There isn’t one clear winner for everyone.

For sleep, I take magnesium glycinate/bisglycinate a couple of hours before bed. It’s my preference, although it hasn’t been established as the best form for sleep. L-threonate also has some interesting, early research for sleep and cognition.

Some other considerations to keep in mind:

• Look for elemental magnesium on the label.

• The adult upper limit is 350 mg/day from supplements and magnesium-containing medications (excluding food). That limit primarily reflects gastrointestinal side effects. Smaller doses throughout the day may improve absorption and be easier on your stomach.

• Athletes and frequent sauna users may need slightly more, because magnesium is lost through sweat.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Rhonda Patrick gets asked about magnesium a lot. Her short version:

Start with food: leafy greens, nuts, seeds and legumes. Supplements are for when your diet falls short.

Citrate, glycinate and chloride are decent options and absorb better than oxide. There's no one clear winner for everyone. Check the label for "elemental" magnesium, and keep supplements under 350 mg a day, because more than that is mostly a gut problem.

She also says people who sweat a lot can lose more of it. Plenty of us on the tools sweat all day in summer, so it's worth getting the food side right first.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Insulin resistance can begin within days of overeating, and the first warning sign is a rise in insulin, well before blood glucose or the scale gives anything away.

Healthy men with normal metabolism were fed a large surplus of a typical American diet, about half of it carbohydrate, for a single week. Their blood was checked every morning after an overnight fast, and their fasting glucose never budged, which by the usual standards would mean their metabolism was perfectly fine.

Their insulin told a very different story. Fasting insulin rose by the second day and kept climbing every day after that, ending the week about two and a half times higher than where it started, and by then the men's bodies were taking up only about half as much glucose in response to insulin as they had at the beginning.

This is the pattern I see over and over, where a steady flood of food, much of it carbohydrate, pushes insulin up and keeps it up, and the cells respond by turning down their sensitivity to it, so that chronically high insulin is driving the very insulin resistance it later gets blamed on.

It also shows why fasting glucose is such a poor early test, since these men would have passed a routine checkup at the very moment their insulin was climbing and their cells were becoming resistant to it.

If someone wants to protect their insulin sensitivity, it's clear that keeping insulin from running high, by not overeating, and particularly not overeating carbohydrate, matters well before blood glucose or body weight shows any change.
hits.draft_en:
Ben Bikman shared a study that's worth knowing about.

Healthy men were fed a big surplus of a normal American diet, about half carbs, for one week. Their fasting blood sugar never moved. By the usual check-up standards they were fine.

But their insulin rose by day two and kept climbing. By the end of the week it was about two and a half times higher, and their bodies were only taking up about half as much sugar in response to insulin.

His point: blood sugar is a late warning. If you want to protect yourself, don't keep overeating, especially carbs. Ask your doctor about a fasting insulin test too.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Fructose has a reputation as the sugar that goes straight to the liver, but it also reaches the gut first, and a short study in young, healthy adults showed how quickly that can matter. Three days of eating more fructose, with total calories held the same, was enough to raise bacterial endotoxin in their blood.

Blood from the gut drains straight to the liver, so what happens in the gut and what happens in the liver end up closely connected. In this study, researchers swapped some of the complex carbohydrate in a standardized diet for either fructose or glucose for three days at a time, kept calories steady, and gave everyone a washout period in between.

After the fructose days, endotoxin in the blood went up, and so did ALT, an enzyme that rises when liver cells are under strain, while markers of nitric oxide, which our blood vessels rely on to relax, went down. The immune cells in the blood also turned up the receptors that recognize endotoxin, leaving them primed and ready to react. None of this happened with the same amount of glucose, and nobody's weight changed with either sugar.

Endotoxin is a piece of the outer wall of certain gut bacteria, and normally very little of it gets past the intestinal lining. Fructose appears to loosen that lining and to favor the kinds of bacteria that make endotoxin, and once endotoxin reaches the blood, the liver is the first organ to meet it. Repeated exposure like this is one of the paths toward fatty liver and insulin resistance.

Three days is a shorter stretch than many people's usual week of sodas, juice and dessert, which is what makes the speed of this change worth noticing.

If someone is trying to protect their liver and their metabolic health, it's clear that the type of sugar matters, and cutting back on fructose-heavy foods and drinks helps protect the gut lining and the liver even when calories stay the same.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Ben Bikman shared a study that's worth knowing.

Young, healthy adults swapped some of their carbs for fructose for just three days, same calories. Bacterial toxin in the blood went up. So did ALT, a liver strain marker. Same amount of glucose didn't do it, and nobody's weight changed.

Three days. That's less than a normal week of soft drink, juice and dessert for plenty of people.

If you want to look after your liver, the type of sugar matters, not just the calories.

Japan has one of the lowest obesity rates in the developed world. By the standard used almost everywhere else—BMI of 30 or higher—only about 4.6% of Japanese adults qualify. In the United States that number sits near 40%. Walk the streets of Tokyo or Osaka and the contrast is obvious: people are simply smaller.
Yet diabetes tells a different story. Age-adjusted prevalence sits around 8%, with more than 10 million adults affected. It is lower than the American rate, but strikingly high for a population that barely has obesity by international standards. The usual explanation—too much body fat—does not fully fit.
A large part of the answer lies in muscle. Skeletal muscle is the body’s primary glucose sink, responsible for roughly 70–80% of the glucose cleared under the influence of insulin. Less muscle means less storage capacity, even when total body weight looks favorable. East Asian populations, including the Japanese, tend to carry less skeletal muscle mass than Caucasian populations at the same BMI. They also store relatively more fat inside the abdomen and have, on average, a smaller reserve of insulin-producing beta cells. The result is that metabolic trouble can appear at BMIs in the low-to-mid 20s rather than the 30s.
Japanese studies repeatedly show the same pattern: people with low muscle mass plus a larger waist have several times the diabetes risk of those with more muscle and less abdominal fat. Diabetes itself then accelerates muscle loss, creating a cycle. High intakes of refined white rice and modest protein intakes over decades can further limit how much muscle is built and kept. Daily walking keeps overall weight down, but it does not always build the absolute muscle mass that functions as a large glucose buffer.
The Japanese example is useful precisely because it separates thinness from metabolic resilience. A low number on the scale is protective against the extremes seen in high-obesity countries, yet it is not enough on its own. Muscle is not optional equipment. It is the main organ that decides how much glucose stays in the blood after a meal. Where that organ is chronically undersized, diabetes risk remains higher than body weight alone would predict.

For decades, the story went like this: depression was a chemical imbalance, specifically low serotonin, and SSRIs fixed it by boosting that neurotransmitter. It was simple, marketable, and repeated so often it became medical common sense.

Then, in 2022, a team led by psychiatrist Joanna Moncrieff published a systematic umbrella review in Molecular Psychiatry. Instead of running one new experiment, they pulled together the major existing reviews and meta-analyses covering the main lines of serotonin research—levels in blood and spinal fluid, receptor binding, the serotonin transporter, genetic studies, and tryptophan-depletion experiments. 

The data involved tens of thousands of people.

What they found was striking for its absence. There was no consistent evidence that people with depression have lower serotonin activity or concentrations than people without it. Some of the largest, highest-quality genetic studies showed no link between the serotonin-transporter gene and depression, even when stress was factored in. 

Experiments that temporarily lowered serotonin availability did not reliably induce depression in healthy volunteers. In a few areas, the data even pointed the other way, or suggested that long-term antidepressant use itself might be associated with lower serotonin measures.

The authors’ conclusion was direct: the main areas of research provide no support for the hypothesis that depression is caused by lowered serotonin activity or concentrations. They did not claim antidepressants do nothing, nor that serotonin is irrelevant to mood. They simply showed that the classic “chemical imbalance” explanation—the one many patients had been told—was not backed by the accumulated evidence.

The paper landed like a quiet earthquake. For many, it was confirmation of long-held skepticism. For others, it raised uncomfortable questions about what exactly the most widely prescribed antidepressants are doing, and why the simple serotonin story had been so durable. The review didn’t end the debate, but it forced a clearer distinction between what the data actually show and the narrative that had dominated for decades.

James Engel started Ozempic in 2023 to manage his type 2 diabetes. Four months later he woke up with sudden vision loss in one eye. Doctors diagnosed non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION)—a rare “eye stroke” from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve that often causes permanent damage. 

He kept taking the drug, unaware of emerging signals linking GLP-1s to the condition. In October 2024 the other eye went. Now legally blind, Engel quit his job, lost his commercial driver’s license, and can no longer watch his grandkids play baseball or pursue the retirement travel he and his wife had planned. 

His case is not unique. Hundreds of people have filed lawsuits claiming Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound, and other GLP-1 drugs caused sudden NAION and vision loss, and that manufacturers failed to adequately warn patients and doctors. Those claims are consolidated in federal MDL 3163 in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania—roughly 278 cases pending as of early November 2026. Plaintiffs allege failure to warn, design defects, and related theories; the companies deny liability and note the absolute risk remains low. 

On November 9, 2026 the FDA required every GLP-1 product (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, etc.) to add a warning about a potential increased risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section. 

In the agency’s analysis of 126 trials covering more than 134,000 patients, the rate was about 6.4 cases per 100,000 person-years on a GLP-1 versus 3.8 on placebo or other glucose-lowering drugs. Cases have been reported with every marketed GLP-1. The European Medicines Agency had already classified NAION as a very rare side effect of semaglutide (up to 1 in 10,000) and advised stopping the drug if it is confirmed. 
NAION is sudden, usually painless, and typically affects one eye. There is no proven treatment to reverse the vision loss. Risk factors overlap with those of many GLP-1 users (diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, older age, “disc at risk”). Absolute risk is small, but for the people who develop it the consequences are life-altering—as Engel’s story shows.
Patients are advised to report any sudden painless vision change, visual-field defects, or other disturbances immediately and seek urgent ophthalmology evaluation. Doctors are told to consider discontinuing the GLP-1 if NAION is diagnosed unless the benefits clearly outweigh the risk. 
The drugs remain widely used and effective for many. The new labeling and the growing lawsuits simply make one more rare but serious trade-off explicit.

On a clear October afternoon in 1948, newlyweds Harry and Esther Snyder unlocked the doors of a tiny 10-by-10-foot stand in Baldwin Park, California—barely a spit of land across from Harry’s childhood home. 
With $5,000 and a stubborn belief that people deserved better than frozen patties and wilted lettuce, they launched In-N-Out Burger. Harry, a WWII veteran who had spent years in food service, cooked while Esther kept the books from their nearby house. The stand sold roughly two thousand burgers in its first month. 

What set them apart was pure invention. After long days on the line, Harry tinkered in his garage until he built a two-way speaker system—the first of its kind. Customers could pull up, order without leaving the car, and drive out with hot food in hand. (They even handed out sheets of butcher paper to protect laps.) The name In-N-Out captured that simple motion, and California’s modern drive-thru was born. 

Harry’s obsession with freshness never wavered. He inspected potatoes, tomatoes, and onions daily, refused frozen beef, and insisted fries be cut from whole potatoes right in the store. The menu stayed ruthlessly simple—burgers, fries, drinks—while customer requests quietly birthed the famous “secret” menu: Animal Style with grilled onions and extra spread, Protein Style wrapped in lettuce. Growth was deliberate. By Harry’s death in 1976 there were only 18 stores. His son Rich expanded the chain, but family tragedies followed. Still, the Snyders kept it private, never franchised, and treated employees like family. 

Nearly eight decades later the arrow still points to pride. Under granddaughter Lynsi Snyder, In-N-Out operates roughly 445 locations across ten states, with a new eastern headquarters in Tennessee and careful plans for places like New Mexico. Distribution centers ensure every restaurant gets fresh ingredients within a day’s drive—no freezers, no compromises. The Double-Double still tastes like it did in 1948 because the family never stopped believing Harry’s original bet: quality would always outlast speed.

Van Ness rotationplasty: the surgery that turns your foot into a knee
One of the strangest-looking procedures in orthopedics is the Van Ness (or Van Nes / Borggreve) rotationplasty. 
It’s mainly used for bone cancers like osteosarcoma near the knee in kids, or severe congenital limb deficiencies. Instead of a high above-knee amputation, surgeons remove the tumor and the knee joint, then rotate the lower leg 180 degrees and reattach it so the ankle sits where the knee used to be. The foot ends up pointing backward. 
The nerves and blood vessels stay connected. Once it heals, the patient gets a custom prosthesis that the backward-facing foot and ankle slip into. Pointing the foot straightens the prosthetic “knee”; flexing the ankle bends it. You end up with a living, muscle-powered knee joint instead of a passive mechanical one. 
It looks bizarre (and the cosmetic appearance is the biggest downside), but functionally it often beats a standard above-knee amputation: better control, lower energy cost for walking, more durability, and the ability to run, jump, and play sports. Because it’s the patient’s own tissue, it also grows with a child. 
First done in the 1920s–1930s for tuberculosis, popularized by Dutch surgeon Cornelis van Nes in the 1950s, and refined for tumors in the decades since. Still uncommon, still visually wild, and still one of the better functional options when the alternative is losing the knee entirely. 
Weird? Yes. Effective? For the right patient, absolutely.

Long before farms or cities, small bands of humans moved across the landscape following herds. 
They left behind bones, scraps, and the lingering scent of cooked or raw meat around their camps. Wolves, already skilled hunters and scavengers, began lingering at the edges—not as enemies, but as opportunistic neighbors.

The boldest or least fearful of those wolves stayed closer. Over generations, the ones that tolerated human presence better gained a reliable source of leftover meat and fat. Humans, in turn, gained something useful: animals that could help track game, warn of predators, and, in some cases, assist in the hunt. 

What began as scavenging gradually became a partnership. The wolves that thrived nearest humans slowly became dogs.

Both species were built for animal foods. Early humans were adept hunters and scavengers of large game, relying heavily on meat, organs, and fat for energy and nutrition. Wolves were pure carnivores by nature. 

In those early days of domestication, the overlap was clear—dogs ate what humans left behind or shared from successful hunts. The relationship formed around the same core resource: animal protein and fat from the landscape.

Only much later, after agriculture spread, did some dog lineages develop a greater ability to digest starch. The original bond, however, was forged in a world of hunting and scavenging, where humans and their emerging canine companions thrived on a diet centered on meat. 

That ancient overlap still shows in how many dogs prefer and perform well on animal-based foods, and in the enduring partnership between the two species.

Together, these advances connect medical evidence with practical help across the tools teams already use—so they can spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

https://t.co/NI35X8pG57

outsiders.name: Satya Nadella
outsiders.text:
Our ambition with everything we are announcing at Ignite today is to parlay technological advances into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations, and society at large.

Just a few of the things we're announcing:

outsiders.name: Sam Altman
outsiders.text:
6.2 Sol and Astra are out.

These models can do amazing things and are very token-efficient; we hope people will get great value from them.

In particular, 6.2 Sol ultrafast is something I think people will really enjoy. https://t.co/KNjtDKRwj7

outsiders.name: Mistral AI
outsiders.text:
To celebrate Mistral Vibe + Le Chonk becoming the world’s best open model-harness duo, we’re making Vibe free in Europe for the first 3 months. 

(Yes, it’s actually better than GLM / DeepSeek at coding). 

Use code LECHONK via link in 🧵. Limited time, first-come, first-served. https://t.co/bERB9ce6yw

outsiders.name: Sundar Pichai
outsiders.text:
Knowing things → doing things → finding ways to save you time and money

We’re expanding Tasks in Gemini free of charge to hundreds of millions of people in six countries. Powered by Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Tasks lets you hand off everyday life admin directly:

- Forward emails to gemini@google.com to RSVP and add it to your family calendar
- Have Gemini call local businesses to compare price quotes and check inventory (with full transcripts + approval before dialing)
- Check out securely via Google Pay (uses the Agent Payments Protocol - AP2)
- Seamlessly sign in via Google Password Manager

We wanted to make this helpful + secure, we’re also partnering directly with major websites and security providers so it works well for site owners and agents.

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Announcing Perplexity Frontier Research. We are committing at least 10,000 GPUs to work on multi-agent orchestration and continual learning systems with the goal of building an automated researcher. We will publish evals, papers, blogs and open source our models and tooling. We’re actively hiring!

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text: This by Anthropic seems both right & a condemnation of many “agentic solutions” & harnesses being built at companies. Rather than a sprawl of specialized subagents built by different teams, you often get better & cheaper results using one agent to do it all https://t.co/FR52rpGMet

outsiders.name: OpenAI Developers
outsiders.text:
Upgrades, people. Upgrades.

The wait is over, you can now use GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol in Codex and the API. https://t.co/Uz6JF5XAF1

outsiders.name: clem 🤗
outsiders.text:
Introducing Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted 🤗

We adapted Qwen's model specifically for the pi coding agent using reinforcement learning and a LoRA adapter.

The results, measured as pass@1:
🚀 SWE-bench Pro (Hard 51): 29.4% → 62.7%
💻 Terminal-Bench 2.1: 39.5% → 55.8%
⚡ 55–62% fewer https://t.co/HhK1nwdOgl

outsiders.name: Google DeepMind
outsiders.text:
What happens when you put Gemini 4 Carbon to work in the lab? 🔬

Researchers are using our latest model in Google @Antigravity to tackle multi-step problems across physics, math, and the life sciences.

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text: I’ve been using GPT-6.2 Astra prior to launch & I found it very uneven  & weird. On one hand, it was harder to steer & work with than other models. On the other, when given an ambitious project (make a space elevator ride from scratch with Blender & Unity) it could deliver well https://t.co/gc10YRzIkw

virals.text: Thrilled to announce $5B in funding for @IsomorphicLabs to accelerate our mission to Solve All Disease. Gradually, then all at once... https://t.co/ihOS3L9vPC
